items.title: [MacRumors] macOS 27.3 Warns Against Giving AI Apps Full Mac Control
items.content_html:
With the latest macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is giving Mac users more control over the data they share and the access they give to apps, including apps that use AI agents. Apple today informed developers about upcoming changes to the Full Disk Access API and the Device Control and Data Access API.


Here's what Apple says is changing:

  • The current Device Control and Data Access setting will be split into two options that make it clearer to users what they're permitting. The setting is becoming System & App Protection Override and Accessibility.

  • There will be a single method for granting permissions by selecting the app requesting access from a list.

  • Apple will encourage users to grant access to just the specific apps (in System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) required for workflows.

  • Apple will better inform users about the data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are given.

  • Users will have an option to configure apps to ask each time for required access rather than granting an app unrestricted access.

  • There will be a transparency indicator when a requesting app is controlling another app with System & App Protection Override. The indicator will be displayed in the Mac menu bar.


Apple says developers will need to adjust user onboarding and make sure apps can "gracefully handle" access to a limited set of folders or apps when using the APIs being overhauled.


Apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup or the new Accessibility settings for assistive technologies can request entitlements to offer the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3.

Right now, known apps keep their current experience without an entitlement, and app permissions granted by users prior to macOS 27.3 will remain in effect. Mac users will see these changes when approving new app permission requests, and entitlement details are coming soon.

Last month, Apple said it would add "additional controls" for Full Disk Access on Macs because of the risks posed by AI agents. Apple warned that some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that can put users at risk, exposing files, mail, messages, browsing history, and more.
This article, "macOS 27.3 Warns Against Giving AI Apps Full Mac Control" first appeared on MacRumors.com

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI is making software easier to build. Keeping it running is another story
items.content_html:
These days, it almost feels like old news: Developers can now use AI tools to generate code, build features, and make changes in a fraction of the time they once needed. The problem now surfacing across businesses is that once software goes into production, teams still need to monitor, maintain, and fix it. A feature that takes minutes to build can introduce problems that take engineers hours to investigate.

Google’s 2025 DORA report, based on responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals, found that greater AI adoption was associated with faster software delivery but reduced stability. While the researchers didn’t establish that AI-generated code directly caused more outages, their findings suggest that companies can produce software faster without necessarily becoming better at maintaining it.

That raises a critical question for companies investing heavily in AI coding tools: If development keeps getting faster, how much of the work involved in running software can also be automated? A growing group of companies is working to find out, developing AI systems that can investigate failures, identify possible causes, and, in some cases, take corrective action without waiting for an engineer.

MORE SOFTWARE, MORE TO MANAGE

Ishay Yaari, cofounder and CEO of DataAgent, a company developing autonomous remediation software, says the operational side of software development hasn’t advanced at the same pace as coding.

“More code, more frequent deployments, and more infrastructure changes naturally create more potential failure points,” he tells Fast Company.

For site reliability engineering (SRE) teams, that means managing applications and infrastructure that may be changing more frequently. When something fails, engineers must figure out what changed, identify the cause, and restore service.

Consider an application that begins crashing after an update. The cause could be faulty code, an incorrect configuration, insufficient computing resources, or a problem with another service. While monitoring tools may detect the failure immediately, engineers still need to examine logs, review recent changes, and investigate several possibilities before deciding what to fix.

Yaari says companies often respond to growing complexity by adding monitoring tools and collecting more data. That can help engineers see what’s happening, but it can also mean more alerts to investigate without necessarily improving how quickly problems are resolved.

The pressure isn’t necessarily coming from poor-quality AI-generated code. Even reliable code can be difficult to manage when applications, infrastructure, and dependencies are changing frequently.

In a recent analysis of AI-assisted development, Google’s DORA researchers found that developers saved time generating code but spent more time reviewing and verifying it. They also emphasized the importance of testing, feedback, and established engineering practices in turning faster development into better results.

For companies, that means the benefits of AI coding tools may depend partly on what happens after developers finish writing the code, particularly the ability of SRE teams to keep applications running reliably.

GIVING AI THE KEYS TO PRODUCTION

Software monitoring and observability tools have traditionally helped engineers detect problems and understand their causes. Now companies are trying to automate more of the response.

DataAgent is pursuing that approach. Its platform is designed to monitor applications and cloud infrastructure, identify potential issues, and help investigate them. Yaari wants AI to take on more of the operational work engineers currently perform manually.

Some failures have familiar remedies. An application might repeatedly crash because it doesn’t have enough memory. A deployment might fail because of an incorrect configuration. Or a new release might introduce errors that disappear when the system returns to an earlier version.

Companies already use automation to address certain problems through predefined rules. AI could extend that capability by examining the circumstances, identifying likely causes, and selecting an appropriate response.

Yaari says DataAgent’s platform is designed to understand both the infrastructure supporting an application and the application itself, including how services interact, what the application is expected to do, and how its behavior changes after an update.

The aim is to recognize problems that don’t fit a predefined rule. But identifying a likely solution is one thing. Allowing software to make changes to a live application is another.

Consider a deployment that introduces errors. Rolling back to the previous version may restore service, but if the update also changed a database or introduced new dependencies, reversing it could create additional problems. That’s why the ability to act matters as much as the ability to diagnose.

HOW MUCH SHOULD AI BE ALLOWED TO FIX?

In its 2026 State of AI-First Operations report, PagerDuty found that 44% of surveyed organizations required human involvement when AI was used to fix problems affecting customer-facing systems, while 43% required it when coordinating incident responses across teams.

Even companies adopting AI for operational work appear reluctant to give it unrestricted authority over critical systems.

Yaari agrees that some decisions should remain with people. He points to actions such as deleting large amounts of data, disabling security controls, or exposing sensitive information as examples that should require approval.

“The goal is not to remove humans from SRE; it is to remove humans from the repetitive operational work that machines can handle safely,” he says.

Companies must determine which systems an AI agent can access, what changes it can make, and when it must request approval. They also need records of what the agent did, particularly when an attempted fix fails.

Another consideration is the cost of monitoring and observability software. Applications generate vast amounts of logs, performance measurements, and other operational data. Companies pay to collect, store, and analyze that information, often across several platforms. Adding AI can create further expenses if it requires transferring large amounts of data to external services.

Yaari argues that more analysis should happen closer to where applications run. DataAgent is pursuing a distributed approach, with agents deployed within customers’ infrastructure to reduce the amount of data sent elsewhere.

Its published documentation describes local monitoring alongside cloud-based AI analysis and guided incident investigation. Yaari’s responses describe broader autonomous remediation capabilities. The company has not provided independent performance data establishing how much operational work or cost those capabilities can eliminate.

WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ENGINEER?

Yaari expects engineers to spend less time investigating repetitive incidents and more time designing systems, setting operational policies, and deciding what automated tools should be allowed to do.

“The fundamental shift is from people operating infrastructure to people managing autonomous infrastructure,” he says.

That could allow smaller engineering teams to support more applications, but it would also require them to understand how automated systems make decisions—and what happens when those decisions are wrong.

Engineering skills may evolve as a result. System architecture, security, reliability, and the ability to investigate unusual failures could become more important as routine operational work becomes easier to automate.

Google’s DORA research found that organizations with strong engineering practices were better positioned to benefit from AI-assisted development. The same lesson may apply to AI-powered operations. Companies will still need reliable processes for testing changes, responding to incidents, and evaluating whether automated fixes work.

The software industry has made considerable progress in helping developers produce code faster. Now it’s trying to bring some of that speed to keeping applications running.

If AI eventually handles both, engineers may spend less time performing individual tasks and more time deciding what the systems they build should do, how they should behave, and when a person needs to intervene.

Users add an eligible U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard or American Express card, review the items, total and selected card, then approve each purchase with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint. A payment-network token replaces the card details, which are not shared with the agent or merchant. OpenAI says users retain applicable card rewards and dispute protections, while merchants continue to handle pricing, delivery, returns and customer service. The company also released guidance to help retailers make their sites and payment systems work with agents. OpenAI plans to let users set spending limits and other conditions so agents can make purchases without approval for each transaction. That option is not yet available, and the company has not announced when Wallet will reach other subscribers or countries.

Although only a small share of experts process each token, all experts must remain in graphics processing unit (GPU) memory during inference. The researchers tested HOPE on three open-weight models. On one coding benchmark, they reported that a model pruned by 50% scored 42.3, compared with 41.8 for the unpruned model and 36.2 for a competing pruning method. The study describes HOPE as a training-free compression method, meaning it does not retrain the model after pruning.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] A cyberattack forces you to pull the plug. Can your business keep running?
items.content_html:
The recent cyberattack on European supermarkets sent the temperature in some Swedish freezers to a sweltering 131 F (55 C). The Dutch grocery chain Ahold Delhaize warned that a separate hack could strip up to 250 million euros ($277 million) from sales, and wipe as much as 100 million euros off operating profit in the fourth quarter. 

This recent spate of cyberattacks around the world, including a staggering $6.3 billion heist at the crypto exchange Binance, lays bare a blind spot in many boardrooms. Directors too often ask whether attackers can break into their systems. They should also be asking whether the business can take the hit and keep running.

Boards should assume attackers will get through. It’s a question of when, not if. And when they do, can the business still fulfill orders, pay staff, and keep critical facilities open? 

Too rare

Unfortunately, this is often not the case in the companies that I deal with. I recently worked with a board that had rightly grown more worried about cyber threats, and drafted in a former spy to carry out a cyber audit. The contractor ran penetration tests, hacked a few of the firm’s products, and found holes in its defenses. 

That’s fairly typical. The audit tested whether hackers could penetrate the company’s defenses. But it stopped short of testing whether the business could ride out a breach. And this is the gap I see running through many companies. 

Sometimes, stopping an attack from spreading means shutting down the very systems that keep you operating. 

Ahold Delhaize took some of its own websites and apps down as a precaution after the cyberattack, cutting off online shopping for some customers. The Dutch group contained most of the disruption within two weeks and it was getting back to normal once it reported third-quarter results. In Belgium, it had online shopping back up and running just a week after disclosing the breach. 

Contrast that with Marks & Spencer, the British retail stalwart. After a breach in April 2025, it stopped taking online clothing orders for a spell of 46 days. And when orders finally resumed, only part of its clothing range was available.

If you have to pull the plug on your own systems to contain a breach, how will you keep serving customers? 

The AI factor

AI is only raising the stakes. It’s my view that cyber threats have changed more in the past six months than in the previous six years. But many companies haven’t caught up.

Some of the newest crop of AI models are spotting security flaws that their predecessors missed, and have worked out how to exploit some of them. 

Take Anthropic’s Mythos Preview, which scored about 83% on a cybersecurity benchmark, compared with roughly 67% for the company’s previous best model, Claude Opus 4.6. Anthropic says it spotted thousands of security flaws, many of them serious, including in every major operating system and web browser. Worrying indeed. 

Last week, OpenAI released GPT‑6 Cyber to vetted customers. The model is designed to find security flaws and test whether they can be exploited.

The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre says the gap between a flaw becoming public and attackers exploiting it has already shrunk to just days. And it predicts that AI will compress that window further still, giving defenders even less time to patch the holes.

The most recent spate of supermarket hacks came on the heels of a similar hack of fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets. The result was piles of spoiled food, and fires even broke out.

Following that breach, Danfoss, the Danish industrial company that made the temperature controls, urged its customers to update their software and hardware. But just weeks later, hackers hit retailers using Danfoss controls again. This time, stores in several European countries were hit, including Sweden and Ireland.

Some fared better than others. Carrefour said it had installed updates and secured its connections after the first wave of attacks, steps it credited with curbing the numbers of its Belgian stores hit. Acting on the first warning helped Carrefour blunt the next attack.

Some retailers left their refrigeration systems exposed. That’s unacceptable. But even with tighter security, you still need a way to trade when the systems you depend on go dark.

What to do

Protect the operations you can least afford to lose. Then drill your teams on how to keep them running through an attack. When the malware designated NotPetya hit Maersk in 2017, the shipping giant handled about 80% of its usual volume manually. Staff taped paperwork to containers and took orders through personal Gmail accounts.

Consider a distribution center that needs to keep essential goods moving. Ask one team to fulfill a handful of priority orders without its usual order system or company email. Can staff confirm orders using a secure offline list and an agreed backup channel, check stock by hand and arrange transport? Have them log each dispatch on paper and check those logs against the order system once it’s back online.

When the drill ends, ask how much of the usual workload the team handled safely, for how long, and where it got stuck. Give each fix an owner and a deadline, then run the drill again.

Find out how long you can keep serving customers with your systems down. A real attack is a brutal way to get the answer.

items.content_html: Microsoft’s investigation into its global Microsoft 365 outage points to backend servers that failed automated health checks, leaving the remaining systems struggling with heavier traffic. Engineers’ attempts to restart servers also failed when traffic returned, while a later network change exposed a problem introduced during an earlier capacity upgrade. The failure disrupted Exchange Online, Microsoft’s cloud email and scheduling service, and affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot across government, business and public services. Microsoft said neither a cyberattack nor artificial-intelligence agents caused the incident. Engineers gradually restored services while working through an email backlog. Digital Trends reported that engineers deployed a patch targeting an authentication and routing component. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said the company would publish a review with a step-by-step timeline and repair measures. Microsoft’s notice to customers said it would issue a preliminary report within two business days and a final report within five.

items.content_html: AI coding editor Cursor said an attacker used an access key exposed at its inference provider, Fireworks AI, to access internal data and place tampered Anthropic Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s marketplace on October 29. The two versions remained available for about 11 hours. As many as 5,000 users who requested them may have received the builds, but that figure does not confirm successful infections. The attacker found credentials in historical coding-agent traces from users who had not enabled Privacy Mode, then accessed selected Cursor services. Cursor said the attacker did not affect customer code repositories or official releases. It has cut off Fireworks access, rotated credentials and rebuilt the marketplace. It believes the incident is contained and advises affected developers to follow its cleanup guidance.

items.title: [stheadline.com] White House AI task force urges 12-month cyber liability relief
items.content_html: The White House’s artificial intelligence task force urged federal agencies to limit penalties for companies that voluntarily report cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents in good faith, recommending at least 12 months of relief. The recommendation is not an order, and agencies have not committed to adopting it. The task force said existing enforcement standards may be outdated as AI changes cyber threats and that fear of penalties could discourage reporting. The group also backed long-term renewal of the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, which provides liability protections for sharing threat data, and discussed a voluntary process for reporting AI-related incidents. The recommended relief applies only to cyber incidents, not to every AI-related safety failure.

items.title: [Théoo] On techno-solutionism
items.content_html:
I've been seeing more techno-solutionist talk online lately. Maybe it's just my algorithms that decided to show me more of that or maybe people are actually talking more about it. Either way, it made me think about this subject and it's implications, and also made me quite scared.

When I talk about techno-solutionism in this post, I mean it in relation towards climate change. Here's a definition to make sure we're all thinking about the same thing when reading this article.

Techno-solutionism is the idea that we will fix the climate crisis by using technology so we don't have to change our way of life.

Now let me preface by saying that I personally don't believe in techno-solutionism and I will develop why in this post. But even if you believe in it, I think you should read-on as my goal is not to judge or critisize but rather to ask questions and I think your answers would be as interesting as anyone else's.

The solutions that are often brought up in techno-solutionist discussions are Carbon Capture, AGI that will find the solutions for us, Geoengineering and Nuclear fusion.
As of now, none of these solutions are a reality. We are seeing progress in each of them, but they still pose many challenges that we are yet so solve.

The question then is, do we want to bet on things that we don't know for sure will ever become a reality? Because, you might strongly believe these will someday exist but you can't prove that they will. It's just a belief.
Personally, I don't want to throw the life of future generations of living beings to a bet.

Now, let's say this works and we actually figure these things out! What tells us that we'll figure them out in time?

Because while we are working on these solutions, the climate crisis is still going on. Living beings are quickly dying and becoming extinct, and even if you don't care about non-human forms of life, humans are dying too.

Are we as a species really willing to let so many other forms of life die for us to keep up with our current way of life?

Are we, the people living in privileged countries willing to keep exploiting other humans for our own profit and well being?

And can we really feel well and happy about how we'll live in a world where we have "fixed" the climate crisis but can still feel all the damages it caused?

Maybe your answer to all of these is yes, and maybe you'd even tell me that it's also possible that we will figure techno-solutions in time.
So let's say you are right about this, let's say that by 2050, we've found solutions that allow us to go to negative carbon emissions!

Then the question is, are you willing to let companies decide of the quality of the air you breathe?
Because since we live in a capitalist society, the companies running carbon capture machines and doing the geoengineering required to keep our current living standards will want to make profit.

They won't do it for the sake of being nice to us, when is the last time you've seen a company just be nice and gain profit off of it?

Now you could argue that we are already trusting companies for many really important things like electricity or transport of goods. But these aren't vital things.
People used to live without electricity and they would grow their own food, but no one would be able to live without breathable air.

My personal opinion on this is that I am definitely not ok with putting my survival and the survival of future generations in the hands of any company. And don't get me wrong, I would love to keep up the life that I currently have, it's so comfortable. And I so wish that every human going forward would have the same comfort of life that I have. But I simply don't think it is possible.

Maybe you are ok with the idea that only a few living beings will have a great life at the cost of all others, in which case, business as usual is perfectly fine. But I am not.

I believe that it is more than overdue that we start rethinking our future.
I don't want of a future where machines are what is keeping us alive like we are some sort of ill person surviving only because of their ventilator.

Let's use what we know and are sure of to build a new collective imagination. A world where yes, we will have lost a lot of our current comfort at the benefit of more equality, more mutual aid, more connexion to nature and each other, more time to think and dream.
A world where we can wake up every day without being stressed by an imminent wall that we seem to being sprinting towards at great speeds.

Sure, we won't be able to eat McDonalds, order stuff from the other side of the world for only a couple bucks and get it delivered the same day, drive a car to go buy food at the big nearby mall, travel for a few hundred euros/dollars to go virtually anywhere in at most 2 days, change phone as we please, etc

But isn't that worth it for the certainty that we and other livings, will be able to live for millennia to come?

We should stop being trapped in our current vision of the world and I'm hopeful that someday we'll look back on this time period like we are looking back on how they lived in the middle ages.

I would love to hear about you opinion on this subject, even if you disagree. So please feel free to send me a mail so we can discuss this matter further.

Have a nice day :))

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] A remote employee refused 160 webcam photos a day. Her employer fired her
items.content_html:
Across the workforce, employer surveillance is growing increasingly common, even though it is widely disliked by employees. According to the American Psychological Association, employee monitoring increases workers’ stress and decreases their reported mental health. A Canadian study found that surveillance in the workplace makes employees feel more pressured, less satisfied with their job, and like their privacy is being violated.

AI may now make this problem worse. These negative outcomes are the consequences of more traditional surveillance methods like keyboard tracking and email monitoring. Considering that, what would the psychological impact be of learning that an employer will now use AI to take 160 photos of an employee’s face every day?

A recent New Jersey lawsuit alleges that an employer was trying to do just that, and fired its employee when she refused to agree to this monitoring. The plaintiff in this case, Glennis Von Sander-Timinski, worked for Sutherland Healthcare Solutions, which provides healthcare services outsourcing. The suit states that she had been working at home with no issues since 2018, and had achieved positive performance reviews during that time. 

However, everything changed in August when her company told her that they would be using a new tool: Sentinel AI. This software would take a photo of her through her webcam about every three minutes over the course of the day, for a total of about 160 photos per day.

Von Sander-Timinski objected to this with the worry that it would increase her stress level, and therefore trigger her underlying lupus. According to the Lupus Foundation of America, stress can be a significant trigger of lupus flares, which can result in fevers, rashes, and sores. Her doctor wrote a note to her employer arguing that the facial AI monitoring should be changed to be “intermittent or less frequently, as it is causing worsening of anxiety and flaring her systemic lupus erythematosus.”

However, Sutherland Healthcare was not willing to compromise and gave her an ultimatum. She could agree to the AI monitoring, come into the office every day, or be fired. Returning to the office was not feasible as she lives in Atlantic County, on the opposite side of New Jersey from her employer’s office in Clinton. The lawsuit estimated that her daily commute would have been a total of six hours long.

Therefore, on September 8, Von Sander-Timinski was fired. She had worked at Sutherland for over a decade, since it acquired the company she previously worked for in 2013. 

“Our client’s employer failed to engage in the interactive process required under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination and denied a reasonable accommodation that would have allowed Ms. Von Sander-Timinski to continue performing her job duties successfully, as she had done for years prior to the implementation of this monitoring system,” said Von Sander-Timinski’s lawyers in a statement to The Bergen Record.

While many states currently do not have any laws against employer surveillance, some states, such as New York, Connecticut, Delaware, and California, are beginning to set boundaries for companies. Earlier this year, Maine also passed a law that bans surveillance within an employee’s home unless it is deemed necessary.

New Jersey is similarly looking to pass a law that would regulate AI electronic monitoring tools in the workplace. It would mandate that AI-powered surveillance would need to be approved by an independent auditor and would limit where and when monitoring can be active. 

While this bill is still under discussion, it could potentially help employees like Von Sander-Timinski avoid similar situations in the future. For now, in the vast majority of states, if an employer decides to implement facial monitoring, employees will have little option but to smile for the camera.

—By Chloe Rosenberg, Freelance Writer

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Microsoft’s massive outage puts its AI-driven layoffs under scrutiny
items.content_html:
Microsoft’s massive service outage on Thursday left businesses and government agencies scrambling to access critical services. It also came at an awkward moment for the tech giant, which has undertaken an extensive initiative to reduce its workforce even as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence.

Recent efforts to trim the company’s head count included extending buyout offers to 9,000 U.S. employees in April and 60,000 employees in four countries in October. It also laid off 4,800 workers in July, mostly in its sales and Xbox divisions. Last month, The Information also reported that leadership in Microsoft’s Azure cloud division had discussed cutting costs by at least 20%; Microsoft denied the report.

Meanwhile, the company is pouring billions into AI infrastructure. Earlier this year, it projected roughly $190 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, much of it driven by the enormous computing demands of AI and cloud services.

Fast Company has reached out to Microsoft for comment.

There is no evidence that either the workforce reductions or AI investments directly contributed to Thursday’s disruption. But the incident raises a broader question for Microsoft and the tech industry: As businesses shrink their workforces and increasingly rely on AI to boost productivity, are they also risking the reliability of their existing products? 

Workforce reductions and restructurings can push out experienced employees who understand how a company’s systems work, including any longtime bugs or quirks, and who know how to respond when something breaks. Even if layoffs don’t directly cause technical problems, the loss of institutional knowledge can make those problems harder to solve.

Enacting such reductions while also adapting to a rapidly changing technology like AI may be especially risky. As companies reorganize around these new tools, fewer resources may be available to maintain and troubleshoot existing systems. 

The challenge is particularly acute for massive tech companies such as Microsoft, whose sprawling infrastructure includes decades-old systems alongside cutting-edge AI services.

Microsoft and many other firms are also betting that AI allows smaller teams to maintain or increase their productivity. But that doesn’t necessarily translate into greater reliability. Keeping complex systems running requires experienced employees who can anticipate failures and understand how different components interact, especially when something goes wrong.

And for technology companies, the burden falls not only on humans but on the machines themselves. As companies expand AI services and add new layers of infrastructure, their systems become more complex, and potentially more vulnerable, which could make outages more difficult to prevent or contain.

While the root cause of this week’s disruptions remains to be seen, the incident is a reminder of the stakes at hand in Microsoft’s transformation. To succeed, it not only has to accomplish more with fewer workers, but must also do so without sacrificing the services its customers already depend on.

The company said attackers exploited the privilege-escalation flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123039, against a couple of dozen customers. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 13. Attackers first used the PHP2Shell remote-code-execution vulnerabilities to access Check Point gateways, then exploited the local flaw to install web shells and the TSGA backdoor. items.title: [Pinterest Engineering Blog - Medium] How Pinterest Improved Analytics Agent Compliance with Loop Engineering
items.content_html:
Skyler Zheng | Software Engineer II; Chris Moradi | Staff Data Scientist; Lu Liu | Staff Software Engineer; Aman Gairola | Manager II; Michael Chau | Manager II

The Compliance Problem

Compliance means following the right steps at the right time

Pinterest’s Analytics Agent helps teams answer questions such as “How did query latency for the ads reporting pipeline change last week?” It searches the company’s data ecosystem, analyzes the relevant information, and recommends an answer or course of action.

Not every question requires the same steps. We call the agent compliant when it identifies and follows the steps that apply. Improving compliance is intended to make answers more consistent and reduce the risk of incomplete or inaccurate results. Examples include:

  • Read the data-discovery skill when it needs help finding the right tools or sources.
  • Inspect table metadata before writing SQL to learn what the columns mean, which filters are required, and whether the table has important usage notes.
  • Search every relevant source type, including tables, dashboards, and metrics, rather than stopping at the first useful result.

These are three examples from a broader set of compliance rules, and whether they apply depends on the question. If a user provides the appropriate table, the agent may not need the data-discovery skill, while an open-ended question may require a broader search. The agent must decide which rules apply and follow them when needed.

That flexibility also makes compliance difficult. When the agent skips a required step, it may stop at the first table it finds, miss an important filter in the metadata, or overlook a certified metric with a more authoritative definition. It could then confidently report that “latency is down 4.2%.”[1] The answer may sound reasonable while using the wrong definition, pipeline stage, or reporting window.

Why manually revising the agent’s instructions was not enough

Measuring noncompliance showed us where the agent failed, but not how to fix it. After parsing existing chat logs, we found that table searches occurred more than ten times as often as chart and dashboard searches.[2] For a separate rule requiring the agent to read the data-discovery skill, compliance reached only 64% across a broader set of chats even after we manually revised the agent’s instructions.[3]

It was often difficult to predict which change would improve the agent because the model could interpret reasonable instructions in unexpected ways. One guardrail designed to keep the agent within its intended scope seemed reasonable:

Scope: Only answer questions within your domain. For unrelated requests, politely decline and suggest that the user try a general-purpose assistant.

The guardrail produced an unexpected response:

User, paraphrased: “What are the cloud storage costs for this table, and how long is its data retained?”

Agent, paraphrased: “This is outside my domain. Please try a general-purpose assistant.”

Although the topic sounded like specialized infrastructure, it was an in-scope data question because the agent had access to relevant storage data. The agent had misclassified the question and declined without searching. We identified the cause only after trying and evaluating several changes.

Manually revising the agent’s instructions therefore became a process of trial and error, with no reliable way to know whether a change would generalize or break something else. We needed a repeatable process that could propose a change, test it, and use the results to guide the next attempt. That cycle of proposing, testing, and learning became the foundation of what we call loop engineering. We explain the full approach later in this article. Before building it, however, we first needed test suites that defined success and protected behavior that already worked.

Build the Evaluation Framework

Start with paired test suites

We built a separate pair of test suites for each compliance rule we wanted to improve, such as reading the data-discovery skill or searching all required source types. A focused LLM labeler answered two questions for each chat, and humans reviewed the labels:

  1. Does this compliance rule apply to this chat?
  2. If it applies, did the agent follow this compliance rule?

We used the first answer to assign each chat to a suite. If the rule applied, the chat went into the required suite. If it did not, the chat went into the skip suite. We then compared the agent’s behavior with that expectation. A chat passed if the agent followed the rule when required or skipped it when it was not needed. These pass and fail labels gave us a baseline for comparing future versions.

Both suites are necessary. If we tested only required cases, a system prompt telling the agent to “always search dashboards” could earn a perfect score even when a dashboard was irrelevant. We saw this tradeoff in testing. A change that made the agent search dashboards more aggressively fixed one chat where a dashboard was required, but it also triggered dashboard searches in two chats where they were not. The required suite showed the improvement; only the skip suite revealed the two new regressions.[2]

Together, the suites gave the loop a balanced goal: follow the rule when a question requires it, and avoid unnecessary actions when it does not.

Protect unrelated behavior with regression tests

These two suites covered only the rule we were tuning. We also needed to protect everything else the agent already did well. For that, we used a much larger regression suite and rejected any change that pushed its performance below the required level.

Once we could measure progress, the next challenge was helping each iteration learn from the ones before it.

Design the Tuning Loop

Why persistent sessions and Ralph Wiggum loops both fell short

Our first design kept one agent session open across every iteration. The full history helped the agent make better decisions early, but the context grew with every attempt. Later iterations became more expensive and less reliable.

The second design used a memoryless pattern often called a Ralph Wiggum loop. Every iteration started with a fresh context window, reducing the context sent to the model and lowering the estimated model cost by about fivefold.[4] The tradeoff was that it often repeated earlier mistakes because it had no memory of what had already failed.

One design remembered too much; the other remembered nothing. The final design needed fresh context without losing the lessons from earlier iterations.

Fresh context with structured memory

Every iteration now starts a fresh session and reads a compact, structured handoff. The handoff records:

  • Current results: Scores for every test suite, including validation cases not used for tuning.
  • What is failing: The cases that still fail and their likely causes, helping the agent address a broader pattern instead of one example at a time.
  • The best change so far: The highest-performing change from earlier iterations, which becomes the starting point for the next one.
  • What not to repeat: Previous approaches that reduced performance or failed to solve the problem.
  • Possible test problems: Cases that no candidate has passed, which may indicate an issue with the test rather than the agent.
  • What must remain stable: Test suites that are not allowed to regress, along with the file and line limits for the next change.

The handoff preserves decisions rather than conversation history. Each new session receives the evidence it needs, while the context stays small enough to remain useful.

How the tuning loop works

For each rule, we split the required and skip cases into tuning and validation sets. The tuning cases guide improvements to the agent, while the validation cases test those improvements on examples that did not guide them. A final holdout set stays untouched until the end. Alongside these rule-specific cases, the larger regression suite checks that the agent’s other capabilities still work.

Each iteration follows the same process:

  1. Draft up to four changes to the Analytics Agent’s system prompt, skills, context layer, or tools.
  2. Evaluate every candidate on the same small sample and select the highest-scoring one. If the scores are effectively tied, prefer the change that adds less prompt context and modifies fewer lines.
  3. Evaluate the winner on the full tuning and validation suites.
  4. Apply the acceptance checks, then keep or revert the change.

The loop repeats until it reaches its targets, with a preset budget serving as a safety limit. When the run ends, it evaluates the final result on the holdout set.

Reject changes that improve the wrong thing

A higher tuning score is not enough to keep a change. It must also pass three independent safety checks:

  • Repair/break gate: Did the change fix more cases than it broke?
  • Acceptance critic: Does the change address a general pattern, or does it hard-code an answer from the test set?
  • Regression guard: Did the change reduce performance on a test suite that was not allowed to regress?

The checks make acceptance deliberately conservative. A higher score is not useful if the change overfits the test cases or damages another capability.

We also limit what the loop can change. Each proposal may modify only the agent’s system prompt, skills, context layer, and tools. It is capped at a few files and a few dozen lines, with the limit shrinking over the run. Changes outside those boundaries are reverted. This prevents the loop from modifying application code to make its own tests easier to pass.

The shrinking limit also favors small, targeted changes over unnecessary rewrites. Without that constraint, an agent may rewrite a prompt that already works. Amazon’s Promptimus reports the same tendency in its edit mode.

Measure Real Improvement

The run that fooled us

With the test architecture and safety checks in place, the design appeared ready. Our first large run reached 89.3% compliance across its tuning and validation cases.[4] The iteration history told a less impressive story. Most of the gain came from the first accepted change, and iterations 21 through 30 added nothing.

The plateau raised a more fundamental question: when a score moved by one or two cases, was the change real or simply normal model variation?

Despite similar totals, 10.3% of cases changed verdict between runs.[2] Because gains and losses nearly canceled each other out, the aggregate score hid substantial case-level variation.

Learn from individual cases, not only the score

Evaluating every candidate on all 223 cases would take too long, so we first run each one on the same sample of about a dozen cases. With a 10% flip rate, roughly one result in a sample that size may change by chance. That is why we do not rely on a small score increase alone.

The overall score tells us whether performance moved, but individual cases tell us what changed. The loop records which cases changed from fail to pass and which changed from pass to fail. The next iteration uses those results to identify what improved, what broke, and what to address next. Validation cases and the broader regression suite provide additional evidence before the loop accepts a change.

Results: small changes backed by strong evidence

The loop improved compliance in chats where each rule was needed while preserving performance in the skip and regression suites.[3] In other words, a change had to fix existing failures without breaking cases the agent already handled correctly.

The improvement in searching every relevant source type came from a backend change to the Analytics Agent’s search process. Reaching it required two labeled datasets, a dozen loop iterations, and two verification runs. Most of the work went into identifying a change that improved compliance without introducing regressions.

From Prompt Engineering to Loop Engineering

The Analytics Agent now interprets experiment results, respects restricted-data access, builds dashboards, writes reports, and continues to take on new responsibilities. As these capabilities expand, a change intended to improve one workflow can affect how the agent handles others, sometimes introducing new failures.

That is why we moved from one-off instruction changes to loop engineering. People define the goals, evaluation criteria, and safety boundaries. The loop proposes changes, tests them against real failures, and rejects those that introduce regressions. The same process can target other goals, including consistency, latency, and accuracy, as the agent evolves.

Loop engineering turns failures from real user chats into tests that guide changes to the agent. By keeping only changes that improve compliance without damaging existing behavior, it gives us a repeatable way to make answers more reliable as the Analytics Agent evolves.

Acknowledgements

None of this would have been possible without the people who shaped and supported this work. We thank Attila Dobi for design reviews that strengthened the loop; Jason Coffman for the Analytics Agent capabilities and infrastructure; Bryant Xiao for sponsorship and engineering guidance; Yi Wu and Laura Palmer for product vision and direction; and J.C. Zhong, Yufei Dong for the real-world evaluation data and infrastructure.

Footnotes

[1] Illustrative example; not actual Pinterest data.

[2] Pinterest internal evaluation data, global, July to September 2026. Search figures count tool calls, not successful retrieval. One trial per case, and the LLM labeler is not calibrated against human labels. All runs used one base model at one reasoning setting (Claude 4.7 Opus Fast), so results may not hold across models.

[3] Same source as [2]. The 64% figure is the compliance rate across a broader population after the agent’s instructions were manually revised; it is not a before-and-after comparison. The skill-read suite was a separate 41-case dataset built entirely from known failures, so its baseline was 0% by design. The expected-benefit column describes what we expect each rule to improve; we have not measured answer quality directly.

[4] Same source as [2]. The 89.3% is a pooled pass rate over the run’s tuning and validation cases, with most of the gain landing at the first change and nothing kept after iteration 20. The cost comparison is an internal estimate of model inference cost, not a controlled benchmark.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Hackers use 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to steal continuous integration secrets
items.content_html: A campaign dubbed wfx-loot used stolen credentials from 4,837 GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 repositories and plant code designed to steal developer and cloud secrets. Security researchers confirmed the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories. A separate analysis counted malicious commits in 8,093 public repositories, but that does not mean the code executed in each one. The attackers tested access with pull requests titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” then briefly inserted a roughly 1,500-line script into GitHub Actions workflows or npm installation hooks. The script sought GitHub, cloud, package-publishing and AI-service credentials. Attackers often reverted the changes and deleted workflow logs. The campaign relied on valid stolen account tokens, not a flaw in GitHub Actions. Researchers said the operation was still active on Nov. 12, with new probe requests and malicious code still appearing. They advised repository owners to revoke compromised access, rotate every secret available to affected workflows and check cloud accounts for persistent access.
